questions.q: What are the four required behaviors of the chain-reader capstone project, as defined in this lesson?
options: Validated config from .env, a real chain read (block number + balance), clean formatted output with correct exit codes, and typed Result<T> error handling instead of an unhandled crash
A Solidity smart contract, a React frontend, a database, and a payment processor
Only printing "Hello World" to the console
Deploying a token to mainnet
questions.explain: The lesson defines exactly four requirements: validated config, a real on-chain read, clean output with correct exit codes, and typed failure handling — all built from Chapters 5-6 material.

questions.q: Why does the lesson deliberately keep the capstone's scope to a CLI script rather than a full DApp with a frontend and smart contracts?
options: Because frontends and Solidity are impossible in TypeScript
Because a full DApp would require skills (Solidity, frontend frameworks, deployment tooling) this course never taught — those are covered by later courses in the Blockchain Engineer path
Because command-line tools are always more valuable than web apps
Because Express servers cannot call RPC endpoints
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly scopes the capstone to what Chapters 5-6 actually taught, noting that Solidity, frontend, and deployment tooling are the subject of later courses in the path, not this one.

questions.q: Which lesson's pattern does chain-reader's config.ts file use to validate RPC_URL from the environment?
options: Lesson 36's Express error-handling middleware
Lesson 30/34's zod schema validation of process.env, loaded via dotenv
Lesson 31's REPL
Lesson 35's fs/promises file caching
questions.explain: config.ts is explicitly described as using the zod-validated env config pattern from Lessons 29/30/34, not raw process.env access.

questions.q: What counts as the capstone's "definition of done" per this lesson?
options: The script compiles, regardless of whether it ever successfully runs
It prints the current block number and an address's balance against a real RPC endpoint, handles bad input/config with a clear error and non-zero exit code, and never trusts process.env directly
It has at least 100 lines of code
It is deployed to a cloud server
questions.explain: The lesson's definition of done lists exactly these checkable conditions: real successful output, graceful handling of bad address/RPC URL with a non-zero exit code, and validated config.

questions.q: What is described as the capstone's optional stretch goal, not required for a complete capstone?
options: Writing a smart contract in Solidity
Wrapping chain.ts's logic in the Lesson 36 Express server to expose GET /balance/:address as a real HTTP endpoint
Deploying to a Kubernetes cluster
Rewriting the project in Python
questions.explain: The lesson names the Express wrapper from Lesson 36, exposing the balance lookup as an HTTP endpoint, as an optional extension beyond the CLI tool that's actually required.
